A function that sorts, pushes to, or assigns into its argument changes the caller's data. The caller can't see that from the call. If the parameter has a read-only type, TypeScript rejects those changes in the function body, and the signature promises the caller that the value comes back unchanged.

The check is deep, so a `readonly` array of objects that can be changed is still reported. Strings, numbers, and other primitives are always fine, and so are functions.

{/* Generated by src/codegen/lint-rule-docs.ts. Do not edit this section. */}

## Configure

Off by default. This rule needs types, so turning it on makes `bun lint` type check your code first.

```toml bunfig.toml
[lint.rules]
"@typescript-eslint/prefer-readonly-parameter-types" = "error" # or "warn"
```

Every option, set to its default:

```toml bunfig.toml
[lint.rules]
"@typescript-eslint/prefer-readonly-parameter-types" = ["error", {
  allow = [], # list of strings or objects
  checkParameterProperties = true,
  ignoreInferredTypes = false,
  treatMethodsAsReadonly = false,
}]
```

{/* End of the generated section. */}

## Examples

Reported:

{/* bad {"count": 3} */}
```ts
function total(prices: number[]) {}

function rename(user: { name: string }) {}

function names(users: readonly { name: string }[]) {}
```

Not reported:

{/* good */}
```ts
function total(prices: readonly number[]) {}

function rename(user: Readonly<{ name: string }>) {}

function names(users: readonly { readonly name: string }[]) {}

function repeat(text: string, times: number, done: () => void) {}
```

## Options

| Option | Default | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `allow` | `[]` | Types that are accepted as they are. |
| `checkParameterProperties` | `true` | Check constructor parameters that declare a field, such as `private items: string[]`. |
| `ignoreInferredTypes` | `false` | Skip parameters that have no type annotation. |
| `treatMethodsAsReadonly` | `false` | Accept methods that aren't marked `readonly`. |

Each `allow` entry is a type name, or an object that also says where the type comes from: `{ "from": "file", "name": "Draft" }`, `{ "from": "lib", "name": "Date" }`, or `{ "from": "package", "name": "Draft", "package": "some-package" }`.

A `Date` is reported by default:

{/* bad */}
```ts
function format(date: Date) {}
```

With `allow: [{ "from": "lib", "name": "Date" }]` it's accepted:

{/* good {"options": [{"allow": [{"from": "lib", "name": "Date"}]}]} */}
```ts
function format(date: Date) {}
```

A callback's parameter often gets its type from the function you pass the callback to, which you might not control. Here `row` is a `string[]`, so it's reported:

{/* bad */}
```ts
const rows = [["a", "b"], ["c"]];
rows.forEach(row => console.log(row.length));
```

With `ignoreInferredTypes: true` it's skipped:

{/* good {"options": [{"ignoreInferredTypes": true}]} */}
```ts
const rows = [["a", "b"], ["c"]];
rows.forEach(row => console.log(row.length));
```

A method written as `save(): void` can be assigned to, so it counts as something that can change:

{/* bad */}
```ts
interface Store {
  save(): void;
}

function flush(store: Store) {}
```

With `treatMethodsAsReadonly: true` it doesn't:

{/* good {"options": [{"treatMethodsAsReadonly": true}]} */}
```ts
interface Store {
  save(): void;
}

function flush(store: Store) {}
```

## When not to use it

This rule is strict. Most library and DOM types aren't read-only, and every function that takes one is reported until you list the type under `allow`.
